verdict:
AVOID — THE PERMIT-MOAT THESIS IS DEAD, refuted three independent ways from primary sources. This was MY thesis and the court killed it properly; recording that plainly.

(1) THE MOAT HAS AN OBSERVED MARKET PRICE, AND LINDBLAD WAS THE BUYER. It acquired Torcatt Enterprises Ltda — the Ecuadorian holdco that satisfies the local-ownership rule — plus two ships for $17M, adding 45% to its Galapagos inventory. That marks the ENTIRE Galapagos permit-plus-hull franchise at roughly $55M; even grossed at a 3x control/scarcity premium it is ~$165M against a $2.54B EV, i.e. 2-7%. A moat you can buy, whose price you disclosed because you paid it, cannot support the multiple. The whole thesis rested on cupos being unbuyable.
(2) IT CHARTERS 'SCARCE' BERTHS FROM ITS OWN COMPETITOR. A three-year charter of the Greg Mortimer — Aurora Expeditions' hull — for Alaska 2027-2030. A moat you can rent from the incumbent on a three-year lease is a lease rate, not a moat.
(3) ANTARCTIC CAPACITY IS EXPANDING, NOT CAPPED. Aurora +30% expeditioners, the new Douglas Mawson hull in Nov-2025, HX a record season. The supply cap I assumed does not bind.
(4) AND MANAGEMENT'S OWN CAPITAL IS FLEEING THE MOAT: the next two newbuilds are 120-guest EUROPEAN RIVER vessels on the Rhine-Danube — the most oversupplied segment in cruising. When the operator allocates its marginal dollar away from the scarce asset, the scarcity claim is answered by revealed preference.

WHAT THE RESIDUAL ACTUALLY IS: an operating business earning ~$16-18M of pretax income AT 91% OCCUPANCY, THE BEST IN A DECADE, against $47.25M of annual note interest and an Altman Z of 0.84. Red's phrase is the right one — 'an operating lease on other people's ships wrapped in a brand license'.

BLUE PARTIALLY OVERTURNED RED ON PRICE, and I take blue's band. Red normalised to $12-14 using mass-market comps; blue's correction is that RCL/CCL multiples are the wrong comp set for a luxury operator, and the defensible band on honest comps is $15-21 — still ~40% below tape, but the reopen gate must be EV/EBITDA <12x on a NON-PEAK year, not red's <10x, which 'would never print'.

THE DIVERGENCE TEST WAS RUN AND WE FAILED IT — which under the new doctrine is the correct kill: 'no divergence from the street on the operative number'. We are not disagreeing with anyone. That, not the analyst count, is why there is nothing here.

reopen_gates: PRICE: $15-21 (blue's band, overturning red's $12-14 — mass-market comps were the wrong set for a luxury operator). Gate restated as EV/EBITDA <12x on a NON-PEAK year; <10x is a mass-market multiple that would never print here.

MOAT REPRICING is the ONLY path back to a moat-based valuation: a Galapagos cupo transaction at MUCH more than $17M per berth-equivalent, or evidence Ecuador is retiring cupos. Absent that, the moat is marked at its own transaction price.

CORRECTION_20260818_expansion_framing:
ADJUDICATOR CORRECTION (principal challenge: 'why is expansion not good?'). I CONFLATED TWO QUESTIONS and wrote the verdict as though capacity expansion were bearish. It is not.
WHAT EXPANSION LEGITIMATELY REFUTES, and only this: the claim that supply is LEGALLY FROZEN while demand compounds. Operators adding hulls falsifies a regulatory-cap premise. Finding 3 is valid AS A REFUTATION OF THE MOAT.
WHAT IT DOES NOT SHOW: that the business or the market is deteriorating. Capacity grows because operators expect demand — normally the bullish read.
AND OUR OWN EVIDENCE CONTRADICTS THE BEARISH FRAMING, which neither bench reconciled: expedition_inventory found ZERO fare cuts across all 72 itineraries, 59.6% of departures sold out (departure-weighted), and the only concession anywhere is a deposit-terms easing. Set that beside Aurora +30% expeditioners and LIND's own +12% capacity and the honest reading is SUPPLY EXPANDING AND BEING ABSORBED WITHOUT PRICE DAMAGE — a healthy growing market. If expansion were outrunning demand, fare cuts would appear FIRST; that is precisely what the connector was built to detect and it found none.
THE BEAR CASE, RESTATED CORRECTLY — it is about THIS OPERATOR, not the industry: (i) an 18.7x multiple for a business whose permits mark at 2-7% of EV because it BOUGHT them and disclosed the price (independent of expansion); (ii) $16-18M pretax at 91% occupancy, the best in a decade, against $47.25M of annual interest and an Altman Z of 0.84 — in a market where supply responds to demand, excess returns get competed away and this balance sheet cannot absorb that; (iii) capital allocated to Rhine river boats, the most oversupplied segment in cruising.
SECTOR CONSEQUENCE, AND IT RUNS THE OTHER WAY: demand absorbing 12-30% capacity growth at full fare is a reason to look HARDER at eco-tourism, not to close the lane. The question becomes WHO CAPTURES THE GROWTH — likely whoever is lowest-cost or best-capitalised. LIND is neither: it charters hulls from a competitor and its interest exceeds its pretax income. The AVOID at $32.77 and the $15-21 band both STAND; only the reasoning is corrected.
